## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Khurappajātaka* (Ja 265) is a narrative within the Pali Jātaka collection. Its opening verse begins with the incipit *Disvā khurappe ti* [Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha delivered the tale while residing at Jetavana to admonish a bhikkhu who had abandoned his striving (*ossatthaviriya*), reminding him that in ancient times the wise exerted energetic resolve even in pursuits that did not pertain directly to ultimate liberation [Fausböll 1879].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a master forest guide or leader of forest protectors (*ārakkhikajeṭṭhaka*) [Fausböll 1879; Zimmermann 2006]. When hired to safeguard a merchant and his caravan of five hundred wagons travelling through the wilderness, the hero resolutely strikes and overcomes (*paharitvā*) a band of five hundred robbers, safely escorting the caravan to safety [Zimmermann 2006; Hazra 1994]. The text has been cited in modern discussions examining Buddhist ethics regarding the use of force in defense of others [Zimmermann 2006].
